title: Just sitting, again
hookLine: sitting with no object at all, as Dogen taught

cards: In a monastery hall in China, rows of monks sit in silence. One of them is nodding. His head drops, jerks up, drops again.

The abbot, a teacher named Rujing, comes down the row and stops in front of him. Near the sleeper sits a visitor from Japan, Dogen. What the abbot says next, the old accounts tell us, turned Dogen's life.
This path met Dogen's just sitting once before, a long way back. Today, again: shikantaza.

teach.b: In the story, Rujing tells the dozing monk, in substance: sitting is dropping off body and mind. Why are you sleeping? Sleep is one way of escaping the sitting.
Rujing's words point to another way of meeting it: not leaving, not dozing, and not holding on either. Dropping off. The accounts of Dogen's life say that at those words something opened for him.
He went to Rujing's room and said that body and mind had dropped off. Rujing confirmed it, and then added, so the story goes, that the dropping off itself should be dropped off.
Nothing to hold onto, not even the breakthrough.

teach.h: NO COUNT, NO QUESTION, NO GOAL.
teach.b: What Dogen brought home was shikantaza, just sitting: no counting, no question, no image, no goal set out in front. Sitting with no object at all.
It sounds easy, and it can be very hard, because there's nothing to do and nowhere to hide. Now look at the week. The sutras went back on the shelf.

teach.h: THE WEEK'S PIECES, AND THEN NONE.
teach.b: Then the meditation school. The base and the straight back. The hands.
The eyes. The count. Each was a support, and each is still there in shikantaza: the posture stays, the thumbs still touch, the eyes still rest half open.
What drops away is the last tool, the count.
Only sitting is left: this breath, this room, this body. Just this.

how: In Soto Zen, which looks back to Dogen, shikantaza is a central form of zazen, sat in silence facing a wall, often in periods marked by a bell.

o: sitting up through the night without any sleep
sitting until the mind goes completely blank
just sitting, with no object or method at all

games.q: just sitting, again: tap the pairs.
p: the abbot who scolded the sleeper

s: in the story, Rujing lets the dozing monk sleep
he scolds him: sitting is dropping off body and mind.
in shikantaza the posture is dropped along with the count
the posture stays; only the method falls away.
Rujing told Dogen to drop even the dropping off
nothing to hold onto, not even the breakthrough.

games.q: you're the abbot Rujing. a monk in the meditation hall is nodding off. what do you do?
o: let him sleep; rest matters too
scold him: sitting is dropping off body and mind
hand him a question to work on
games.why: Rujing scolds the sleeper, and the accounts say Dogen, sitting nearby, awakened at those words.

practice: Take the week's posture, a stable base, back straight and relaxed, hands in the oval, eyes half open, and count a few breaths if you need to land. Then let the counting go, and don't replace it with anything.
When a thought comes, it comes; when it goes, it goes; don't follow it, don't fight it, just sit.

wordCard.voice: Shikantaza. Japanese for just sitting, nothing but sitting: Dogen's way of zazen, with no object at all. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: just sitting, nothing but sitting; Dogen's word for zazen.

carryVoice: Your line: just this. A whole week of sitting, down to two words. A week on the cushion, done.
